16. Thus, the contents or a letter written by a co-conspirator, giving an account of the conspiracy, is relevant against the other even though not written in support of or in furtherance of it. (Illustration of section 10). Therefore, the existence of a fact of conspiracy must be proved; secondly, there should be prima-facie evidence of the existence of the conspiracy; thirdly, a prima-facie case cannot be made out by mere proof of intention of two or more persons to do an unlawful act or a lawful act by unlawful means; and finally, after the existence of the conspiracy has been established, the particular accused against whom evidence is sought to be led in must be proved to have been a party to the conspiracy. 

 44. When a witness is contradicted with his earlier statement recorded by the police in course of investigation, the only effect that it can have is to reduce the evidentiary value of his testimony in court and make the witness unreliable on the point on which he is so contradicted. The credit of a witness is impeached by proof of former statement with any part of his evidence which is liable to be contradicted. When a witness contradicts his previous statement on a material point the evidentiary value of that statement is destroyed and court shall discard the evidence of that witness so far as it relates to that statement. The High Court Division has totally ignored the suggestions given to PWs 5, 6, 7, 17 and 32 and the admission of PW 48 on those points, and took the evidence of PWs 5, 6, 7, 17 and 32 in chief as the uncontroverted evidence. Reference in this connection may be made the cases of Nazir Hussain vs Muhammad Shafi, 17 DLR (SC) 40 and Abul Kalam Azad alias Ripon vs State, 58 DLR (AD) 26. 

 59. The High Court Division failed to notice that the defence objected to the reception of the photo copy of a letter, Exhibit X-1, filed by PW 48 and it illegally took it into consideration. It was said, one Mr Joydeb Mojumder wrote a letter to the Police Commissioner who did not come forward or anybody from the High Commission Office to prove it and the prosecution did not give any explanation for withholding him. It also did not explain the reason for not filing the original copy. Where the contents of any document are in question, either as a fact in issue or a sub-alternate principal fact, the document is the proper evidence of its own contents, and all derivate proof is rejected until its absence is accounted for. If objection to the admission of secondary evidence is taken at the time of its production, it may be within the power of the party tendering the evidence to correct the irregularity and prove the original, or to show that the secondary evidence is really admissible in the circumstances of the case. 

 85. In Bhubani Sahu, the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council taking section 30 of the Evidence Act was of the opinion that a confession of a co-accused is obviously evidence of a very weak type. It does not indeed come within the definition of evidence contained in section 3 of the Evidence Act. It is not required to be given on oath, nor in the presence of the accused, and it cannot be tested by cross-examination. It is a much weaker type of evidence than the evidence of an approver which is not subject to any of these infirmities. "Section 30, however, provides that the Court may take the confession into consideration and thereby, no doubt, make it evidence on which the Court may act; but the section does not say that confession is amount to proof. Clearly there must be other evidence. The confession is only one element in the consideration of all the facts proved in the case; it can be put into the scale and weighed with the other evidence". 

 "The fundamental of a criminal trial is that the accused shall be presumed innocent and that he is not required to adduce evidence to prove his innocence, but the entire burden of proof of his guilt lies on the prosecution alone and till that time the presumption of innocence, whether the case is before the trial court or at higher forums In a criminal trial determination of a disputed fact is the main task before the court and such determination is dependent upon consideration of answers given by the prosecution in their cross-examination. Cross-examination is therefore indispensably necessary to bring out desirable facts of a case modifying the examination-in-chief or establishing the cross-examiner's own case. The object of cross-examination is twofold, to bring out desirable facts of a case modifying the examination-in-chief on establishing the cross-examiner's own case. 

 192. The learned counsel for the accused-appellant has challenged the reliability and acceptability of the oral evidence also adduced by the prosecution raising several pleas. He has submitted that the PWs on whom the prosecution has relied much for proving the charges against this accused-appellant were examined by IO under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure after an inordinate delay and has argued that this long delay in recording the 161 statements of the prosecution witnesses has made the whole projection case doubtful. In support of this argument also the learned counsel has cited a decision of the Appellate Division in the case of Bangladesh (State) vs Paran Chandra Baroi reported in 6 BCR (AD) 225. The learned counsel has also drawn our attention to the fact that some of the material witnesses did not state to the investigating officer some material facts which they stated before the court and has argued that these omissions in the 161 statements of the prosecution witnesses make their evidence before court unreliable. The learned counsel has cited two decisions also made in the case of Khalil Khan vs State of Madhya Pradesh reported in AIR 2003 467 and in the case of Nazir Hussain vs Muhammad Shafi reported in 17 DLR (SC) 40 in support of this argument. The learned counsel for the accused-appellant has challenged also the legality of examination of PW 32 the wife of the deceased by the investigating officer under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure over telephone. Admittedly, the last IO of this case examined the PW 32 who was residing in Kolkata over telephone. Mr Anisul Haque has argued that there is no provision in any law all owing examination of any witness under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure over telephone and, as such, the examination of PW 32 by the IO over telephone has been illegal and that this fact also has made the evidence of this PW 32 before the court doubtful. Mr. Anisul Haque has made submissions challenging the credibility of PW 5, PW 6 and PW 19 also. He has argued that all these three PWs were not trustworthy at all, that they were procured by the police and deposed before the court as they were tutored by police. The learned counsel has made submissions to the effect also that in this case the High Court Division relied upon certain alleged circumstances, namely, (i) jealousy between the accused-appellant and the victim regarding courting of love of Samanja, (ii) the abscondence of this accused-appellant and (iii) several alleged conversations over mobile phone between this accused-appellant Yasin Rahman @ Titu and accused Alamgir on the day of occurrence in finding the complicity of this accused-appellant in the murder of Jibran Tayyabi and has argued that in fact none of these alleged circumstances has been proved in this case by any cogent evidence. The learned counsel has submitted that this accused-appellant never absconded, rather he went to London for continuing his study there while he was not made an accused in this case and that when he came to know that he was made an accused in this case he wanted to come back and surrender before the court for defending himself, but could not do so as his passport was cancelled. The learned counsel has claimed also that the alleged mobile phone calls between this accused-appellant and accused Alamgir on the day of occurrence has not been proved at all, that the alleged breakup of the mobile phone calls of this accused-appellant produced by the prosecution the exhibit-16 show that one Alamgir Chowdhury and not the accused Alamgir was the owner of the other mobile phone that the High Court Division committed wrong in relying on this alleged breakup of the mobile phone calls the exhibit-16 and came to the wrong finding that on the day of occurrence this accused-appellant Yasin Rahman @ Titu had numerous mobile phone calls with accused Alamgir and took this fact as a circumstance in support of the prosecution case. The learned counsel has argued that the High Court Division without examining and considering the questions as to admissibility and acceptability of the confessional statements, credibility of the witnesses, reliability of their evidence, and the probability and proof of the alleged circumstantial evidence put reliance on these confessional statements and all other evidence adduced by the prosecution and consequently made a wrong decision as to guilt of the accused-appellant. Before concluding his argument the learned counsel for the accused-appellant has submitted also that from the cross-examination of the PW 48 the last IO of this case it transpired that this IO had some grudge towards this accused-appellant and the other members of his family and has argued that this fact also reasonably cast doubt on the prosecution case.
